# AirSQL Help (all pages)

> AirSQL is a free, open-source Mac app (macOS 13.1 or later, Apple silicon and Intel) for MySQL and MariaDB: connections direct or through SSH tunnels, jump hosts and proxies, a SQL console, a data grid with safe editing, schema tools, client tools (mysql, mysqldump), compare and reconcile, and access for AI agents over MCP at the level the person at the Mac sets for each connection. Nothing is written to a server without the person's Run, Apply or approval, and agents never see saved passwords.

- Install: `brew install --cask kleash/tap/airsql` (or the zip from https://github.com/kleash/airsql/releases).

Every page of AirSQL Help (https://kleash.github.io/airsql/), then the agent guide.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/

# AirSQL Help

AirSQL is a Mac app for MySQL and MariaDB. It is in development: these pages grow with it.

- [Install AirSQL](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/install.html): with Homebrew or from the download.
- [Getting started](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/getting-started.html): add a connection, find your way around the window.
- [Settings](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html): the look, the editor and grid, safety checks, agents and client tools.
- [Check SQL before it runs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html): the sheet that shows every change first.
- [Trust a server](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html): servers whose certificate macOS doesn't know.
- [The SQL log](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html): every statement AirSQL sends, with passwords masked.
- [Read-only queries](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html): what an agent's query may do, and why one is refused.
- [The SQL console](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html): write and run SQL, results, transactions, history and the SQL log.
- [Connections and routes](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html): add and edit connections, SSH tunnels, jump hosts, proxies and folders.
- [Browse a server](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/navigator.html): the tree, the database view, table commands, find text and the process list.
- [Change tables, views and routines](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html): the table editor, views and routines as CREATE code, and the ER
  diagram.
- [Export, restore, copy and import](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/client-tools.html): your mysqldump and mysql, or AirSQL's own export and runner; copy
  to another server; CSV import.
- [Compare two databases](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/compare.html): structure and data, side by side, and a sync script you review first.
- [AI agents](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/agents.html): let Claude Code, Gemini CLI or Claude Desktop read your schemas and run read-only queries, at
  the access you choose.
- [Keyboard shortcuts](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/shortcuts.html): every command's shortcut.
- [Privacy and security](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/privacy-security.html): what AirSQL connects to, where passwords are kept, what agents may do.
- [Troubleshooting](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/troubleshooting.html): when a connection fails, and how to report a problem.

Every button and menu command says what it does when you hold the pointer over it.

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/install.html

# Install AirSQL

AirSQL needs macOS 13.1 or later, on Apple silicon or Intel. It is free, and it needs no account.

## With Homebrew

```sh
brew install --cask kleash/tap/airsql
```

Later, `brew upgrade --cask airsql` updates it.

## From the download

1. Download **AirSQL-X.Y.Z.zip** from the [latest release](https://github.com/kleash/airsql/releases/latest).
2. Open the zip, then drag **AirSQL** to your **Applications** folder.
3. Open AirSQL. Apple has checked it (it is notarized), so it opens like any app.

To check the download first, see [Check a download](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/privacy-security.html#check-a-download).

## Remove AirSQL

Drag AirSQL from Applications to the Bin (with Homebrew: `brew uninstall --cask airsql`). Your connections and settings
stay in `~/Library/Application Support/AirSQL`, and saved passwords in your Keychain (the item named
`com.kleash.airsql` in Keychain Access), until you delete them. `brew uninstall --zap --cask airsql` deletes the
settings too.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/getting-started.html

# Getting started

## Add your first connection

Choose **File ▸ New Connection…** (⌘N), or **Add Connection…** on the first screen: the connection appears in the
sidebar, and its summary shows where it goes and how it logs in.

Passwords stay in your Keychain. A connection coloured **Production** starts with stricter safety checks
([Settings](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html#safety)).

## The window

- **The sidebar** lists your connections. Click one to see its summary, double-click it to connect, right-click it for
  everything else (Duplicate, Colour, Delete…). Hold ⌘ or ⇧ to select several.
- **The tabs** hold your queries and tables. Double-click a tab to rename it; right-click it to close others or
  duplicate it.
- **The toolbar** shows the connection and database a tab works on, Run (⌘↩), Run All (⇧⌘↩), Explain, and the
  transaction buttons.
- **The status bar** shows the route to the server, its version, an open transaction, the work running now (click it to
  cancel), what agents are doing, and the SQL log. Click an item for details; right-click it to copy it.

## Tips

- Nothing is written to a database until you press Run or Apply.
- ⌘1 to ⌘9 show your tabs; ⇧⌘[ and ⇧⌘] step through them.
- **Help ▸ Report a Problem** opens a form with your versions filled in.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html

# Settings

Open **AirSQL ▸ Settings…** (⌘,). Changes are saved as you make them.

## General

- **Appearance**: follow the Mac's light or dark mode (System), or always use Porcelain (light) or Deep Water (dark).
- **Settings folder**: where your connections and settings are kept. Passwords are in your Keychain, never there.

## Editor and Grid

- The text size of the SQL editor and of the grid.
- **Rows per page**: how many rows a table or result loads at a time (1,000 by default).
- **NULL shown as**: how empty values look in the grid.

## Connections

- **Load details up to … tables**: on a server with more tables than this, a database's columns, indexes and keys load
  when you open it, so connecting stays quick.

## Safety

What asks first before data changes. These are the defaults; a connection can have its own, and a connection
coloured Production starts with a strict preset.

| Setting | Default | Production |
|---|---|---|
| Ask before UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE | on | on |
| Ask before any write from the console | off | on |
| Show the SQL before the grid's Apply | off | on |
| Ask before DROP or TRUNCATE (a database's name is always typed) | on | on, table names typed too |
| Ask before restoring into a database that has tables | on | on |
| Leave DROP and DELETE out of sync scripts unless ticked | always | always |
| Ask before agents change anything | on | on |
| Agents' rows per query and time limit | 10,000 and 30 s | 1,000 and 15 s |
| Warn when a transaction stays open | 15 minutes | 5 minutes |
| Ask before sorting a large table by a column without an index | on | on |
| Warn when closing with an open transaction or pending edits | on | on |

**Restore Defaults** puts every switch back. Read-only is a switch of each connection. Agents can read these settings
but never change them.

## Agents

- **Allow AI agents to use AirSQL**: off until you turn it on. Agents never see passwords.
- **Connections**: what agents may do with each connection: Off (where every connection starts), Schema, Schema + read,
  or Schema + read + analytics; and **Sample rows**, which lets them see a few rows of each table.
- **Exports**: the only folder agents save files in.
- **Add to Claude Code…** and **Add to Gemini CLI…**: show the change to that program's settings that adds AirSQL, and
  make it when you click Add. **Copy** gives the command other MCP clients start.

More in [AI agents](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/agents.html).

## Client Tools

The `mysql` (or `mariadb`) and `mysqldump` (or `mariadb-dump`) programs AirSQL runs. Leave them empty to let AirSQL
find them: it looks in Homebrew's folders, `/usr/local/mysql/bin`, MAMP and your `PATH`, and picks for each server the
tools of its family and version. Under each field the pane says which program and version it found, or why there is
none or it can't be used; **Found** lists every tool on this Mac, and **Find Again** looks again after you install or
update some. See [Export, restore, copy and import](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/client-tools.html).


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html

# Check SQL before it runs

Some changes show their SQL in a sheet before anything runs: applying edits in a table, changing a table's structure,
dropping or renaming, restoring a dump, and sync scripts.

- **Warnings** say what else will happen, such as rows deleted in other tables (ON DELETE CASCADE), or a table whose
  engine can't roll back.
- A change on a **Production** connection says so in red.
- To drop a database (and, on Production, a table), type its name first.
- When an **agent** asked for the change, the sheet names it. Nothing runs until you approve it; **Decline** refuses it.
- **Copy SQL** copies the statements. **Cancel** changes nothing.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html

# Trust a server

When a server's certificate isn't one macOS trusts (it is self-signed, or from your company's own certificate
authority), AirSQL shows its SHA-256 fingerprint and asks before connecting.

1. Compare the fingerprint with the one the server's administrator gave you.
2. If they match, choose **Trust**. AirSQL remembers the certificate for this connection (the editor's TLS tab shows
   it, with **Forget**) and refuses any other.
3. If they don't, choose **Cancel**: you may not be talking to the server you think.

If a trusted server later shows another certificate, AirSQL says so and doesn't connect unless you choose **Trust the
New Certificate**. Do that only when the administrator told you the certificate changed.

## SSH hosts

The first time a connection goes through an SSH host, AirSQL shows the host's key fingerprint the same way. **Trust**
lets ssh remember the key in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`. If the key ever changes, ssh refuses to connect and AirSQL says
which host it was: ask its administrator before removing the old key from `known_hosts`.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html

# The SQL log

AirSQL writes every statement it sends to a server into one file on your Mac, just before the statement goes out.
Use it to see exactly what AirSQL did: what the console ran, what a table edit applied, what the navigator asked the
server for.

## Where it is

`~/Library/Logs/AirSQL/SQL.log`. Only you can read it (file mode 0600). At 10 MB it becomes `SQL.1.log`, replacing the
one before, and a new file starts. It stays on your Mac: AirSQL sends it nowhere.

## What a line says

```
2026-11-03 14:03:12.345 [Shop production main:12] SELECT * FROM orders WHERE id = 7
```

- the time;
- the connection's name;
- the session: **main** (console tabs), **data** (table tabs and their edits), **schema** (the navigator), **agent**
  (AI agents), **tools** (client tools and compare), **cancel** (the short connection that stops a running statement);
- the statement's number in that session. The server sees the same number in a comment at the start of the statement,
  `/* airsql:main:12 */`, so you can find it in the server's process list.

Lines that start with `--` are AirSQL's own notes: connected (server version, thread, TLS), disconnected, connection
lost, reconnected (and whether an open transaction was rolled back), the number of a statement's error, and
"startup SQL (2 statements)".

## What is never in it

- **Passwords you log in with**: they go to the server only during the login, never as SQL.
- **Passwords and keys inside statements**: replaced with `<secret>`, as MySQL hides them in its own logs: the value
  after `IDENTIFIED BY`, `SET PASSWORD … =`, `MASTER_PASSWORD` or `SOURCE_PASSWORD`, `PASSWORD '…'` in `CREATE SERVER`,
  everything inside `PASSWORD(…)`, and the key of `AES_ENCRYPT`, `AES_DECRYPT`, `DES_ENCRYPT`, `DES_DECRYPT`, `ENCODE`,
  `DECODE` and `ENCRYPT`. A value set for a column named like `password` is hidden too.
- **A connection's startup SQL**: only how many statements it had, since it may hold secrets.
- **Error messages**: only their numbers, because a syntax error quotes the statement it failed on.
- **Results**: rows never go into the log.

Very long statements (an import's big `INSERT`) are cut after 60,000 bytes.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html

# Read-only queries

Where only reading is allowed, such as a query from an AI agent, AirSQL first checks that the statement can only
read. The check is strict on purpose: when in doubt it refuses, and it says why in one line.

## What passes

One statement at a time (a `;` at the end is fine):

- `SELECT`, with `UNION`, subqueries and `WITH … SELECT`;
- `SHOW …`;
- `DESCRIBE`, `DESC` or `EXPLAIN` of a table; `EXPLAIN` of a `SELECT` (`FORMAT=JSON` and `FORMAT=TREE` too);
  `EXPLAIN FOR CONNECTION` and a connection number.

## What is refused, wherever it appears

- More than one statement, and every other kind of statement: `UPDATE`, `INSERT`, `SET`, `CALL`, `DO`, `CREATE` and
  the rest, and `WITH …` followed by anything but `SELECT`.
- `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, which runs the statement, and `EXPLAIN` of `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `REPLACE`.
- `INTO` (a file or variables), `FOR UPDATE`, `FOR SHARE` and `LOCK IN SHARE MODE`.
- Optimizer hints, `/*+ … */`: they can lift the server's time limit (`MAX_EXECUTION_TIME`).
- Temporary tables: they can be written even in a read-only transaction.
- Setting a variable with `:=`, and moving a sequence on (`NEXT VALUE FOR`, `NEXTVAL`, `SETVAL`).
- Any function other than the built-in ones that only compute. So `SLEEP`, `BENCHMARK`, `GET_LOCK` and the other
  locks, `LOAD_FILE`, `LAST_INSERT_ID` and the waits for replication are refused, and so are user-defined functions,
  stored functions (`shop.bonus(…)`, or any name AirSQL doesn't know) and function names in quotes.

The text inside executable comments, `/*! … */` and `/*M! … */`, counts as code, whatever server version it names.

## Backslashes and double quotes

The check reads a backslash in a string as the server does: as an escape, unless the session's sql_mode has
`NO_BACKSLASH_ESCAPES`. Double-quoted text with a backslash in it is refused either way: with `ANSI_QUOTES` it is a
name, where a backslash escapes nothing, so the server could end it somewhere else. Write strings in single quotes.

## A safeguard, not the only one

For a hard guarantee, connect agents with a database user that can only read.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html

# The SQL console

A console tab is where you write and run SQL on one connection. Its statements run one at a time, on the connection's
own session, which every console tab of that connection shares.

## Open a console

- **File ▸ New Query** (⌘T), the **+** at the end of the tabs, or **New Query** on a connection's menu opens an empty
  console on the selected connection.
- **File ▸ Open…** (⌘O) opens .sql files, each in a console of its own. You can also drop .sql files on the editor.
- **File ▸ Save** (⌘S) saves the console's text to its file; **Save As…** to a new one. A tab with unsaved text shows a
  dot instead of its close button.
- When you quit, the open consoles are kept, unsaved text included, and come back the next time you open AirSQL.
- **Query ▸ Change Connection…** runs the console's statements on another connection.

## Write SQL

- Keywords, names, strings, numbers and comments have their own colours; the brackets around the cursor are marked.
- **Completion** opens as you type: after FROM or JOIN the tables and views, after JOIN first the joins that foreign
  keys give (`orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id`), after `alias.` that table's columns, after USE the databases, and
  elsewhere the statement's columns, functions and keywords. ↑ and ↓ choose, Return or Tab inserts, Escape closes;
  ⌥⎋ opens it anywhere. It comes from what AirSQL already read of the schema: nothing is sent to the server while you
  type.
- **View ▸ Query Helpers** shows beside the editor the columns of the tables the statement at the cursor names, the
  server's functions by kind, and the keywords. Double-click one to put it in at the cursor.
- **Edit ▸ Find** (⌘F) and **Find and Replace** (⌥⌘F) find in the editor, with **Regular Expression** and **Match
  Case**. With a regular expression, `$1`, `$2`… in the replacement put in its groups. **Replace All** is one change
  that **Undo** takes back.
- **Edit ▸ Comment Lines** (⌘/) comments the selected lines out with `--`, or takes the comment away. **Shift Right**
  (⌘]) and **Shift Left** (⌘[) indent; so do Tab and ⇧Tab on several lines.
- **Query ▸ Format SQL** (⌥⇧⌘F) puts each main clause on a line of its own and reserved words in capitals. It changes
  nothing else: names, values, comments and `/*! … */` code stay exactly as they are, and statements inside a
  `DELIMITER` block are left alone. If it couldn't do that, it leaves the SQL as it was and says so.
- **View ▸ Bigger** (⌘+), **Smaller** (⌘−) and **Actual Size** change the text size for a moment; Settings ▸ Editor
  sets it for good.

## Run it

| To run | Press |
|---|---|
| The statement at the cursor, or the selected text | ⌘↩ (or ⌃F9) |
| Only the selected text | Query ▸ Run Selection |
| Every statement | ⇧⌘↩ (or F9) |
| Stop the statement that is running | ⌘. (Query ▸ Cancel) |

The statement that ran is highlighted for a moment, so there is no "which statement?" question. Statements are split
on `;`, or on the delimiter a `DELIMITER` line sets, and sent one after another; a run stops at the first error.

While a statement runs, the bar above the results shows which one and for how long, with **Cancel**; the status bar
lists it too. Cancel stops only that statement: AirSQL checks the server is still running it before it stops it. A
connection can have a query timeout: a statement that runs longer is stopped the same way, and Messages says so.

Console tabs of one connection share its session, so while one runs a statement the others wait.

## Results and Messages

- Each result set gets a **result tab** under the editor, named after the comment just above its query (`-- Top
  customers` names it "Top customers"), else "Result 1", with its rows and columns. The next run replaces the result
  tabs, unless you **pin** one (right-click it, or Query ▸ Pin Result).
- Double-click a result tab to rename it; right-click it to pin, rename or close it.
- **Messages** lists what each statement did: its rows or the rows it changed, how long it took, the server's
  warnings, or its error and the line it points to (that line is marked red beside the editor). Double-click a message
  to select its statement.
- A result keeps at most its first 100,000 rows; the tab then says it is cut short.

## Transactions

- **Tx: Auto-commit** (the toolbar, or Query ▸ Transaction Mode) commits each statement by itself. In **Manual**, your
  changes wait in a transaction until you press **Commit**, or **Rollback** to undo them. Leaving Manual with changes
  waiting asks first whether to commit them or roll them back.
- **Query ▸ Isolation Level** sets how the console's transactions see others' changes. Until you choose one, the
  server's own applies (usually Repeatable Read).
- While a transaction is open, the status bar says so, with the number of rows changed, and how long it has been open
  once that passes the time set in Settings ▸ Safety.
- Closing the connection's last console with a transaction open asks first: **Commit**, **Roll Back** or keep the tab.

## What asks first

The safety settings (Settings ▸ Safety, or a connection's own) decide which statements ask before they run. The SQL
shows in a sheet, with what it will do:

- an UPDATE or DELETE without WHERE, which changes every row of its table;
- DROP and TRUNCATE; dropping a database needs its name typed, and so does dropping or emptying a table where the
  connection says so (the Production preset does);
- on a connection where every write asks (the Production preset), any statement that may change data.

## History, the SQL log, plans and profiles

- **Query ▸ Query History** (⌘Y) lists the statements run on the console's connection, newest first. Type to search;
  Return or a double-click puts one in the editor at the cursor. Passwords in statements are masked before they are
  kept, as in the SQL log.
- **View ▸ SQL Log** (⌥⌘L) shows every statement AirSQL sent, as they come. See [the SQL log](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html).
- **Query ▸ Explain** (⌥⌘E) shows how the server would run the statement at the cursor, without running it: as the
  server's table, or as a tree (MySQL's own tree; MariaDB's plan made into one).
- **Query ▸ Profile** runs the statement and shows where the server spent its time, step by step, where the server keeps
  profiles (SHOW PROFILE).


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/connections.html

# Connections and routes

A connection is a MySQL or MariaDB server AirSQL remembers: its address, the login, how to reach it (its route) and
a few options. Passwords go in your Keychain, never in AirSQL's files.

## Add or edit a connection

Choose **File ▸ New Connection…** (⌘N), or select a connection and choose **Connection ▸ Edit…**. The editor has five
tabs:

- **General**: a name, the sidebar folder, a colour (Production also turns on the strict safety checks), the host and
  port, or for a server on this Mac its socket file, the user and password, and the database to open. Tick **Ask at
  each connect** to type the user and password each time; they are kept until you disconnect and never saved.
- **TLS**: how the connection is encrypted. **Check the authority and host name** is the safe choice: the server must
  show a certificate for the host name you typed, even through a tunnel. A server whose certificate macOS doesn't know
  shows its fingerprint when you connect (see [Trust a server](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html)). Add an authority file for a
  private certificate authority, and a client certificate and key for a server that asks for one. **PAM or LDAP
  login** allows the plain-text login such accounts need, only over TLS that proves the server.
- **SSH and Proxy**: the route (below).
- **Options**: read-only (writes from the console, the grid and agents are refused), the compressed protocol, a query
  timeout, the databases shown (names or patterns such as `shop, reports_*`), startup SQL that runs after each login
  (for example `SET time_zone = '+00:00';`), and safety checks of the connection's own.
- **Agents**: what AI agents may do with this connection.

**Test Connection** connects with what the editor shows, reports each hop with its time, and disconnects. **Save and
Connect** saves and connects; **Save** only saves.

## Routes

Every route but Direct ends in a private socket on this Mac, in a folder only you can open. AirSQL, the client tools
and Terminal all connect through it, so the route works the same for each.

| Route | What it does |
|---|---|
| Direct | TCP to the host and port, or the server's own socket on this Mac. |
| SSH tunnel | ssh to the SSH host, which connects to the database host. |
| SSH through jump hosts | ssh through each jump host in order, then the SSH host. |
| SSH through a proxy | The first SSH host is reached through an HTTP CONNECT or SOCKS5 proxy (jump hosts optional). |
| Proxy, no SSH | The proxy connects to the database host itself. |

The database host is the name as the last SSH host or the proxy reaches it: often `127.0.0.1` or a private address.

SSH hosts log in with your ssh-agent and keys in `~/.ssh`, a key file, or a password. Whatever the server asks for
besides (a key's passphrase, a password, a code from your phone) appears as a question when you connect; tick
**Remember in Keychain** to save a password or passphrase once the connection works. The first time you reach an SSH
host, AirSQL shows its key fingerprint to trust; ssh remembers it in `~/.ssh/known_hosts`.

Your `~/.ssh/config` still applies: type one of its `Host` names as an SSH host and its settings (user, port, key,
its own proxy) are used, after what the editor sets.

## Import hosts from ~/.ssh/config

**File ▸ Import from ~/.ssh/config…** asks you to pick the file (it opens on `~/.ssh/config`), lists its hosts, and
makes a connection for each one you tick: an SSH tunnel through that host to a database on `127.0.0.1:3306`, which
you can then edit.

## Connect and disconnect

Double-click a connection, or select it and choose **Connection ▸ Connect** (⌘K). The status bar shows each step, hop
by hop, with Cancel. A connection that drops (the network goes away, the server restarts) is marked in the sidebar;
AirSQL never reconnects behind your back. **Connection ▸ Disconnect** (⇧⌘K) asks first when a tab has an open
transaction or edits that aren't applied.

Connected connections are kept alive with a ping every minute, except a session whose transaction has been open longer
than the safety setting allows.

## Folders

Folders group connections in the sidebar. **Connection ▸ New Folder…** makes one (the selected connections move into
it); right-click a folder to rename or delete it (its connections stay). The editor's **Folder** menu moves a
connection.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/navigator.html

# Browse a server

Once a connection is connected, the sidebar shows its databases under it. Each database groups its objects by kind:
tables, views, sequences (MariaDB), procedures, functions, triggers and events, with how many there are.

## Find your way

- **Click** a database to see its tables in the database view: rows, the space their data and indexes take, engine,
  collation, when they last changed and their comment. Click a column's title to sort by it.
- **Click** a table or view to see its rows; **double-click** it (or press Return) to open it in a tab of its own.
- **Click** a routine, trigger or event to see its definition; **double-click** (or **Open**) to open it in its editor.
- **Open Structure** in a table's menu opens the table editor ([Change tables, views and routines](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html));
  **Create Table…** and **New…** make a table or object in the database you right-clicked.
- **Double-click** a database to make it the current one (it shows in bold) and open it.
- **Right-click** anything for everything you can do with it. Every command is also in the **Database** menu.
- Hold ⌘ or ⇧ to select several tables, then drop, empty, check or change them all at once.
- Type a few letters of a name to jump to it, or type in the sidebar's filter (⌥⌘J) to show only what matches. While you
  filter, a connected connection whose name doesn't match shows the objects that do, opened.
- Drag a table or database into the SQL editor to insert its name, quoted for SQL.
- **Refresh** (⌘R) reads the selected database or objects again from the server; with the connection selected, all of it.

On a server with more than 3,000 tables, AirSQL reads only the names when it connects; a database's columns, indexes and
keys load when you open it (a spinner shows on its row meanwhile). Change the number in Settings ▸ Connections.

## Change databases and tables

Every change shows its SQL first ([Check SQL before it runs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html)); nothing runs until you choose to.

- **New Database…** asks for a name, a character set and a collation (the server's own are chosen at first).
- **Drop…** deletes the selected databases or objects. Dropping a database always asks you to type its name; on a
  Production connection, so does dropping or emptying a table.
- **Truncate…** deletes every row of the selected tables. It can't be rolled back.
- **Rename…** gives a table or view a new name. Views and routines that use the old name aren't changed.
- **Copy Table…** copies a table into the same or another database, with its rows or without, or only the rows where a
  condition you type holds (for example `created_at >= '2026-01-01'`). Indexes come along; foreign keys don't.
- **Bulk Table Editor…** moves the selected tables to another database, or changes their engine, or converts them and
  their text columns to another character set and collation.
- **Maintenance** ▸ Analyze, Check, Optimize, Repair or Checksum runs on the selected tables and shows what the server
  said in a tab. Analyze, Optimize and Repair show their SQL first: Optimize rebuilds a table and locks it meanwhile.

A read-only connection offers none of these.

## Find text on the server

**Find Text on Server…** looks for a text in every text column of every table (or of one database), and lists the
tables that hold it with how many rows. It reads each table in full, so it can take a while on a big server: the status
bar shows how far it is, and **Stop** or Cancel ends it. Double-click a table in the list to see its matching rows.
Upper and lower case match as the column's collation says (most ignore case).

## See what the server is running

**Process List** (⌥⌘P, or **Processes** under the sidebar) lists every connection to the server and the statement it is
running, refreshed every 5 seconds (choose another interval, or Off). Double-click a row to read its whole statement.

- **Kill Query…** stops a statement; its connection stays.
- **Kill Connection…** ends a connection, rolling back its open transaction.

Both ask first. Right before it stops anything, AirSQL checks that the process is still running what the list showed
(on MariaDB, that exact statement); if it has moved on, nothing is stopped and AirSQL says so.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/editors.html

# Change tables, views and routines

AirSQL edits a table's structure in a form, and views, procedures, functions, triggers and events as the CREATE
statement that makes them. Nothing changes on the server until you apply, and the SQL that will run is always shown
first.

## The table editor

Open it from a table's **Open Structure**, or make a new table with **Database ▸ Create Table…**. A table editor has five
parts, chosen at the top:

- **Columns**: name, type (the types your server has), length or ENUM values, unsigned, NULL, default, extra (counts up
  by itself, follows updates, or is generated from an expression), collation and comment. Drag rows to reorder the
  columns.
- **Indexes**: primary key, unique, plain, full-text and spatial indexes. Write their columns separated by commas:
  `email(10)` indexes the first 10 characters, `created_at DESC` sorts down.
- **Foreign keys**: this table's columns, the table they point at and its columns, and what happens on update and on
  delete.
- **Checks**: conditions every row must satisfy. On MariaDB, a check written with a column belongs to that column and
  stays with it when the column changes.
- **Options**: the table's name, engine, default collation, row format, next AUTO_INCREMENT number and comment.

**+** adds a row, **−** removes the selected rows (or press Delete), and a right-click offers the same. New rows show in
green and changed ones in amber until you apply. **Edit ▸ Undo** takes back a change; **Discard** takes back all of them.

Under the lists, the SQL that Apply would run updates as you type. When something can't work yet (a VARCHAR without a
length, two columns of one name, an emoji in a name, which the server would keep as `?`), it says what to fix instead.

## Apply

**Apply** (⌘S) shows the statements in the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html) first. Then they run one at a time on a
connection of their own, and the editor reads the table back from the server.

- MySQL and MariaDB can't roll table changes back: each statement takes effect as it runs. When there are several, the
  preview says so; if one fails, the ones before it stay done, and the editor shows what is left to do.
- A changed foreign key is dropped in a statement of its own first: neither server takes a drop and an add of the same
  key in one statement.
- Dropping a column deletes its values, and changing a column's type converts them: the preview warns about both.
- A large table may be copied while it changes, and writes to it wait until that is done.

## Views, procedures, functions, triggers and events

Open one from the tree, or start a new one from **Database ▸ New Object**. The editor shows its CREATE statement, as the
server keeps it, to edit as text.

- **Runs as** chooses its DEFINER: the account it was created with, or you. Keeping another account's DEFINER needs the
  SET_USER_ID privilege on MySQL, or SET USER on MariaDB.
- Apply runs it in its database, under the sql_mode it was created with (and an event under its time zone), so it
  behaves as before. The footer shows those settings.
- MariaDB replaces it in one statement (CREATE OR REPLACE). MySQL replaces a view the same way, but drops a procedure,
  function, trigger or event first: if the new code fails, the old one is gone. Your code stays in the editor to fix and
  apply again, and **Revert** puts the old code back.
- Renaming it in the code makes the new one and then drops the old one.

## The ER diagram

**Database ▸ ER Diagram** draws a database's tables with their keys. Tables that point at nothing come first on the left,
and each table sits right of the tables its foreign keys point at; lines go from a key's column to the table it points
at. Tables with no keys come last.

Click a table to select it (the arrow keys move between tables), double-click it to open it in the table editor, and
right-click it for **Open Structure** and **Copy Name**. **Export Image…** saves the diagram as a PNG, and **Export
Mermaid…** as Mermaid text, which many docs sites and wikis draw.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/client-tools.html

# Export, restore, copy and import

AirSQL backs up and moves data with your own `mysqldump` and `mysql` (or MariaDB's `mariadb-dump` and `mariadb`)
when you have them, and with its own code when you don't. Every command here is in the **Tools** and **File** menus
and in a connection's right-click menu in the sidebar.

## Which programs AirSQL uses

**Settings ▸ Client Tools** shows the programs AirSQL found and their versions. It looks in Homebrew's folders
(`/opt/homebrew/opt/mysql-client/bin` and the like, on Apple silicon and Intel), `/usr/local/mysql/bin` (MySQL's
installer), MAMP and your `PATH`. Leave the fields empty and AirSQL picks, for each server, the tools of its family
(MariaDB's for MariaDB, MySQL's for MySQL) closest to its version. Choose a program to always use that one.

Each sheet says how well its tool suits the server: **✓ suits the server**, a warning (another family's tool, or an
older version than the server), or why it can't be used (not there, too old: AirSQL needs MySQL 5.7 or MariaDB 10.3
tools or newer). The tool you pick in a sheet is remembered for that connection.

No tools at all? Install MySQL's or MariaDB's client tools (for example `brew install mysql-client`), then choose
**Find Again**. Until then, Export and Run SQL File use AirSQL's own code.

## Export a database

**Tools ▸ Export…** (or right-click a connection ▸ Export…).

1. Tick the databases or tables to export. Space ticks the selected rows; right-click for Include All, Include None and
   Include Only These. One database exports without `CREATE DATABASE`, so you can restore it under any name; several
   databases export whole, each with its own name.
2. Choose the content (structure and data, structure only, data only) and the options: one consistent snapshot
   (`--single-transaction`), binary as hex, gzip, `DROP TABLE` before each table, and views, routines, triggers and
   events.
3. Pick the tool, where to save the file, and any extra options of your own (`--skip-comments`, `--where=…`).
4. The box under the form shows the exact command line. **Copy Command** copies it.
5. **Export**. The sheet shows the table being written, the bytes so far and the time left. **Stop** ends it.

The dump goes into a hidden file next to the one you chose and takes its name only when it is complete, so a stopped
or failed export never leaves half a file.

**AirSQL (built in)** in the Tool menu writes the SQL itself, through a connection of its own: the tables' `CREATE`
statements, their rows as `INSERT`s (binary as hex), then views, routines, triggers and events, all read in one
consistent snapshot. Its files restore with `mysql` or with Run SQL File.

## Restore a dump, or run a .sql file

**Tools ▸ Restore…** runs a `.sql` or `.sql.gz` file with your `mysql` or `mariadb`; **File ▸ Run SQL File…** opens the
same sheet with AirSQL's own runner, which splits the file into statements as `mysql` does (`DELIMITER` included) and
runs them one at a time. Compressed files are read through `/usr/bin/gzip`.

1. Choose the file and the database it runs in.
2. Choose what happens on an error: stop at the first one (what ran before it stays), or go on and count them
   (`--force`).
3. **Restore** (or **Run**).

Before anything runs, AirSQL reads the whole file for the statements that decide where it writes: `USE`,
`CREATE DATABASE`, `DROP DATABASE`, and `SET GTID_PURGED`. When the file switches to another database than the one you
chose, drops a database, or sets GTID_PURGED, or when the database it writes to has tables already, the SQL preview
sheet says so and asks first (Settings ▸ Safety ▸ *Ask before Restore…*). On a production connection it always asks.
Progress is the share of the file read, so it is real for compressed files too.

## Copy to another server

**Tools ▸ Copy to Another Server…** copies databases or tables straight from one connection to another, through a
session on each: no file in between.

- **To** and **Database**: the connection and the database the copy goes into (made if it isn't there). One database
  can take another name; views and routines follow the new name.
- **Replace tables that are there** drops the other server's tables of the same name first. It is off unless you tick
  it, and the SQL preview asks before it runs. Copies to a production connection always ask.
- If a statement fails, the copy stops; what was copied before it stays.

## Import a CSV file

**File ▸ Import CSV…**

1. Choose the file. AirSQL guesses the separator (comma, semicolon, tab or bar) and shows each field's first value.
2. Choose the table. Each column takes a field of the file, matched by name when the first row names the columns, by
   position when it doesn't, or **Leave out** to take its default.
3. **Import**. The rows go in one transaction: if one fails (a duplicate key, a value the column refuses), none of the
   file stays, and the message says which records.

Empty fields become NULL unless you untick it. AirSQL sends the rows as `INSERT`s: `LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` stays off.

## Open the mysql command line in Terminal

**Tools ▸ Open in Terminal** opens Terminal running `mysql` (or `mariadb`) on the connection, in its database.

## Your password stays private

The client tools get the login from a temporary option file that only you can read (file mode 0600, in a private
folder in AirSQL's Application Support folder), passed as `--defaults-file`, so `~/.my.cnf` and `/etc/my.cnf` don't
change where they connect. The password is never on the command line, in the environment, or in the command shown.
AirSQL removes the file as soon as the tool has read it: once a dump has started writing, once a restore is reading
its input, ten seconds after Terminal starts `mysql`; and anything left behind at the next launch.

Over TCP the tools check TLS the way the connection asks: MySQL's with `--ssl-mode`, MariaDB's with `--ssl` and
`--ssl-verify-server-cert`. MySQL's tools check certificates only against a CA file; for a connection without one, or
with a pinned certificate, the sheet says so and AirSQL's own export and runner (which check it as AirSQL does) remain.

Client tools reach SSH and proxy routes through the connection's private socket once AirSQL is connected through them.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/compare.html

# Compare two databases

**Tools ▸ Compare…** (or **Compare…** in a connection's or a database's menu, which starts from it) opens a window
that compares two databases, on the same server or on two different connections, such as production against staging
or MySQL 8 against MariaDB. Connect both connections first: each side then works through its own route, on a session of
its own. The compare only reads; nothing changes until you run the sync script yourself.

## Run a compare

1. Choose the **source** on the left and the **target** on the right: a connection, then one of its databases (or
   type its name). The sync script makes the target like the source; **Swap** turns them around.
2. Choose what to compare: **Structure and Data**, **Structure** or **Data**.
3. Click **Compare** (⌘R). The bar under the setup shows the table and chunk being checked, and **Cancel** (⌘.)
   stops the compare; the statement running on each server is stopped too. The work is also listed in the main
   window's activity list.

The summary says how many tables match, differ in structure, or are only on one side, how many rows differ, and how
much of the data had to come over the network. The list shows what differs first: **only left** and **only right**
for objects on one side, **structure**, **data**, then **match**. Click an object to see it; double-click it to see
its rows when they differ.

## What is compared

- **Structure:** tables (columns, indexes, foreign keys, checks, engine, comment), views, procedures, functions,
  triggers, events and sequences. The **Structure** tab shows both definitions side by side, the lines only one
  side has marked.
- **Data:** the rows of every table both sides have, matched on the primary key, or on a unique key whose columns
  are all NOT NULL. The **Data** tab lists rows **missing** from the target, **extra** in it, and **changed** rows,
  with the cells that differ marked (hold the pointer over one to see the target's value). Tables without such a key
  are still checked as a whole, but their rows can't be matched or synced. Generated columns are left out: their
  values follow from the others.

MySQL and MariaDB write the same thing differently, and the compare reads them alike: `int(11)` and `int`, MariaDB's
JSON (a LONGTEXT with a check) and MySQL's, `CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` and `current_timestamp()`, `NO ACTION` and
`RESTRICT`, check constraints the two servers name differently. Each flavour writes a view's body its own way,
though, so the same view on MySQL and on MariaDB can still show as different.

### Ignore rules

**Ignore Rules** chooses differences the compare doesn't count. All four are on at first:

- **AUTO_INCREMENT Values**: tables' next AUTO_INCREMENT values.
- **DEFINER**: who views, routines, triggers and events run as. The script then leaves DEFINER out, so they run as
  whoever runs the script.
- **Collations and Character Sets** of tables and columns (MySQL 8 and MariaDB have different defaults).
- **Whitespace in Definitions**: spaces and line breaks in bodies, outside quoted text.

### Tables…

After a first compare, **Tables…** lists the source's tables. Untick a table to leave it out, give the target table
it should be compared with when it was renamed there, list columns whose values shouldn't count (such as
`updated_at`), or add a WHERE condition for its rows on both sides. **Leave Out of Next Compare** in an object's
menu unticks it too.

## How the data compare stays fast

Each server sums up the rows of a chunk of the table (10,000 rows by key order) as a row count and a total of 64-bit
row hashes, computed from MD5. Only a chunk whose sums differ is looked at more closely: it is split into smaller
chunks, and for the small ones that still differ each row's key and hash come over, then only the rows that differ.
A million identical rows are checked without fetching any.

The hashes tell apart values that careless checksums mix up: a NULL and an empty string, values moved from one column
to another, `'a'` and `'A'` or `'a '` under a case-insensitive collation, the same text in latin1 and utf8mb4 (which
counts as the same). Both sessions use time zone `+00:00`, so TIMESTAMP values compare by the moment they stand for.
Floats, decimals written with another scale and JSON with other spacing or key order are compared as values.

## The sync script

The **Sync script** box shows the statements for the selected object; **Copy Sync Script** copies them. **Sync
Script…** opens the whole script in a [console](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/console.html) tab of the target named “Sync script”, to read (it can't
be edited there; **Save As…** keeps a copy). It never runs on its own: **Run** in that tab brings the compare window
back with the script in the [SQL preview](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html), where you can copy it, run it on the target, or cancel. It
runs:

1. `USE` the target database and `SET time_zone = '+00:00'`;
2. the structure changes, in order: foreign keys and objects that go or change are dropped first, then new tables,
   `ALTER TABLE`, views (after the views they use), foreign keys, routines, triggers and events. MySQL and MariaDB
   commit each structure change on its own: they can't be rolled back;
3. the row changes in one transaction: DELETE (children before parents), then UPDATE and INSERT (parents first). Each
   statement must change exactly the rows it names; if one doesn't, because the target changed since the compare,
   everything in the transaction is rolled back. Tables on MyISAM, Aria or MEMORY can't roll back, and the preview
   warns about them.

**Destructive steps are left out** unless you tick **Include destructive steps**: dropping tables, columns, indexes,
checks, foreign keys and other objects only the target has, deleting rows only the target has, and column changes
that could cut or refuse values (a shorter type, NOT NULL). Each destructive statement is marked with a
`-- Destructive:` comment, and the preview's button turns red.

Rows of tables only in the source come with their `CREATE TABLE`. New columns of existing tables get their default
values: after running the script, compare again to copy their values. After a sync, AirSQL offers to compare again.

## Export the report

**Export Report…** saves what the compare found as **HTML** (to read or send), **CSV** (every difference on its own
line, for a spreadsheet) or **Markdown** (for a ticket). HTML and Markdown list up to 1,000 rows per table.

## Limits

- More than 100,000 differing rows in one table are reported as too many to list, without sync statements for that
  table: narrow the compare with a WHERE, or copy the table instead.
- Partitioning, row formats and system versioning aren't compared.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/agents.html

# AI agents

Claude Code, Gemini CLI, Claude Desktop and other MCP clients can use AirSQL to read your schemas, run read-only
queries, profile tables and propose SQL for you to run. They work through AirSQL on your Mac, so they see only what you
allow, never your passwords, and can't change data.

## Turn agents on

1. **AirSQL ▸ Settings ▸ Agents**: tick **Allow AI agents to use AirSQL**.
2. Under **Connections**, choose what agents may do with each connection. Every connection starts at **Off**.
3. Add AirSQL to your agent:
   - **Add to Claude Code…** or **Add to Gemini CLI…**: AirSQL shows the exact change to that program's settings
     (`~/.claude.json` or `~/.gemini/settings.json`), and makes it only when you click **Add**, keeping the old file as
     `.airsql-backup`. Restart the program afterwards.
   - Claude Code's plugin: `claude plugin marketplace add kleash/airsql`, then `claude plugin install airsql@airsql`.
   - Claude Desktop: open `airsql.mcpb` from AirSQL's release.
   - Another client: **Copy** gives the command, `/Applications/AirSQL.app/Contents/MacOS/AirSQL --mcp`.

The connection must be connected in AirSQL for an agent to read it.

## Access levels

| Level | Agents may |
|---|---|
| Off | not see the connection at all |
| Schema | read databases, tables, columns, keys and indexes; put SQL into a console tab |
| Schema + read | also run read-only queries and see query plans, within the row cap and time limit of Settings ▸ Safety |
| Schema + read + analytics | also profile tables, get ten times the rows and four times the time, and save results to files |

**Sample rows** (a separate switch) lets agents see a few rows of each table they describe. Only you can change these:
no agent can, whatever it asks.

## What keeps your data safe

- An agent's statement runs only if AirSQL can prove it reads and nothing more: one SELECT, SHOW, DESCRIBE or
  EXPLAIN, without locking clauses, `INTO`, hints or functions such as `SLEEP` ([what passes](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html)).
- It then runs on a session of its own that the server keeps read-only, inside a read-only transaction that is rolled
  back, with a time limit. Even a statement that slipped past the check can't write.
- To change something, an agent puts the SQL into a console tab. Nothing runs until you press Run.
- For more safety still, connect with a database user that can only read.

## See what agents did

The agents' item in the status bar says what they're doing. Click it (or choose **Tools ▸ Agents ▸ Agent Activity**)
for every call since AirSQL opened, with how it ended. A call that reads a database also shows in Activity, where
**Cancel** stops it. **Turn Agents Off** in that popover (or in Tools ▸ Agents) stops them at once.

## Files agents save

With analytics, agents can save query results as CSV or JSON files. They go only to the **Agent Exports** folder in
AirSQL's settings folder (Settings ▸ Agents ▸ Exports ▸ Show in Finder), readable by you alone.

## The fine print

Agents reach AirSQL through a socket in AirSQL's settings folder that only you can open, with a key that changes each
time AirSQL starts. Other programs running as you could read that key too, as with any app of yours.

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/shortcuts.html

HeidiSQL. ⌘1 to ⌘9 show the window's first nine tabs (Tab 1 above is the first). Commit and Rollback have no shortcut,
so a slip of the fingers never commits.

# Privacy and security

AirSQL holds the keys to your databases, so it is careful by default: it talks only to the servers you set up, your
passwords stay in your Keychain, and nothing changes on a server until you say so.

## What AirSQL connects to

Only the database servers, SSH hosts and proxies you add. It has no account, no ads and no analytics, and it doesn't
check for updates by itself (Homebrew does: `brew upgrade --cask airsql`). The Help menu opens pages in your browser.

## Your passwords

- They are kept in your Keychain, never in AirSQL's settings file, in its logs, in the [SQL log](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html) or in
  what AI agents see.
- A PAM or LDAP login sends the password as plain text, so AirSQL uses one only when you turn it on for the connection,
  and only over TLS that proves the server is the right one.

## Your connections

- TLS is checked against the server's real name, also through an SSH tunnel. A certificate macOS doesn't know is shown
  with its fingerprint for you to [trust](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html), and AirSQL warns you if it ever changes.
- Tunnels and proxies end in a private socket on your Mac, never in a network port that other apps or computers could
  use.
- A server can't make AirSQL read files on your Mac (`LOAD DATA LOCAL INFILE` is off), and AirSQL sends one statement
  at a time.
- A lost connection is reported, never quietly reconnected: that would lose an open transaction without a word.

## Your data

- Nothing is written until you choose Run or Apply. Changes show their SQL first
  ([Check SQL before it runs](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-preview.html)), and Apply checks that each change touched exactly the rows it should.
- A connection coloured **Production** starts with stricter safety checks ([Settings](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/settings.html#safety)).

## AI agents

Agents can't use AirSQL until you allow them. Then each connection has its own access level, an agent's queries must
pass the [read-only check](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/read-only-queries.html), and a change it asks for waits for your approval. Agents never see
saved passwords.

## The app itself

AirSQL is signed by its developer, uses macOS's hardened runtime and is notarized by Apple. Its one library, MariaDB
Connector/C with OpenSSL, is built from pinned, checked sources, and every release includes that source and a list of
what is inside (an SBOM). Every change is scanned for known vulnerabilities, leaked secrets and security bugs. More in
[SECURITY.md](https://github.com/kleash/airsql/blob/main/SECURITY.md).

## Check a download

Every release lists the zip's SHA-256. In Terminal, in the folder where the download is:

```sh
shasum -a 256 -c AirSQL-X.Y.Z.zip.sha256
```

Once AirSQL is in Applications, `spctl -a -vvv -t exec /Applications/AirSQL.app` says
`source=Notarized Developer ID`.


---

Source: https://kleash.github.io/airsql/troubleshooting.html

# Troubleshooting

AirSQL says what went wrong in plain words, with the server's own error under **Details**. Here is what to do about
the common problems.

## A connection fails

| AirSQL says | What to do |
|---|---|
| Can't find the server | Check the host name, and that you are on the right network or VPN. |
| The server refused the connection | Check the port, and that the database server is running. |
| The server didn't answer in time | Check the host name and the port: a firewall may be dropping the connection. |
| The server can't be reached from this network | Turn on the VPN, or connect through an SSH host that can reach the server. |
| The server didn't accept the user name or password | Check both. Through an SSH host, the server sees the SSH host's address, and the account must allow that host. |
| This user may not log in from this computer's address | An administrator can allow it (the account's host part). |
| The server only accepts encrypted connections | Turn on TLS for the connection. |
| The server asked for a login method AirSQL doesn't allow on this connection | A PAM or LDAP account: turn on its plain-text login for the connection, with TLS that proves the server. |
| The server blocked this computer after too many failed connections | An administrator can unblock it (`FLUSH HOSTS`). |

## AirSQL asks about the server's certificate

See [Trust a server](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/trust-a-server.html). If AirSQL warns that a certificate has changed and nobody told you it would,
choose **Cancel** and ask the server's administrator.

## "The connection to the server was lost"

AirSQL doesn't reconnect by itself, because a quiet reconnect would lose an open transaction without telling you.
Reconnect when you are ready. Changes you hadn't committed were rolled back by the server.

## macOS asks about the local network

To reach a server on your local network, choose **Allow** when macOS asks whether AirSQL may find and connect to
devices on it. If you chose **Don't Allow**: System Settings ▸ Privacy & Security ▸ Local Network, then turn on AirSQL.

## AirSQL doesn't open

It needs macOS 13.1 or later. Downloads from the releases page and Homebrew are notarized and open normally.

## Report a problem

**Help ▸ Report a Problem** opens a form on GitHub with your AirSQL and macOS versions filled in. **Help ▸ Copy
Diagnostics** copies those versions and the client library's (no names, hosts or paths). The [SQL log](https://kleash.github.io/airsql/sql-log.html)
shows exactly what AirSQL sent: read it before you share any of it, because it holds your queries.


---

Source: https://github.com/kleash/airsql/blob/main/Resources/AgentGuide.md

# AirSQL agent guide

AirSQL is a Mac app for MySQL and MariaDB. Through its MCP server you can read the schemas of the connections the
person at the Mac allows, run read-only queries, profile tables, and propose SQL in a console tab for the person to
edit and run. You never see passwords, and you can't change data, connections or settings: each connection's access
level is the person's choice alone.

## overview

1. `context` first: the connections you may use (name, id, access level, MySQL or MariaDB and its version, current
   database, schema hash, row cap and timeout), the person's active connection and the open console tabs. A connection
   whose access is Off isn't listed; `hiddenConnections` counts them.
2. `get_schema` once per connection: every database's tables in one compact reply. Keep its `hash` and pass it back as
   `if_changed_from` later: an unchanged schema answers `{unchanged: true}` and costs nothing.
3. `describe` the tables you'll query (columns, keys both ways, indexes, CREATE statement, row estimates).
4. `run_queries` with several statements at once; `explain` a slow one; `profile` a table you don't know yet.
5. To change anything, write the SQL and call `open_in_console`: the person reads it, edits it, runs it. Then
   `read_console` shows what they ran and the result or error.

Connections must be connected in AirSQL (by the person) before the database tools work on them.

## access

Each connection has one level, set by the person in Settings ▸ Agents (or the connection's Agents tab):

- **Off** (the default; Production connections start here): invisible to agents.
- **Schema**: `get_schema`, `describe`, the schema resource, `open_in_console`; `read_console` without result rows.
- **Schema + read**: also `run_queries` and `explain`, within the connection's row cap and timeout (Settings ▸ Safety:
  10,000 rows and 30 s by default, 1,000 and 15 s on Production).
- **Schema + read + analytics**: also `profile`, `to_file`, ten times the rows and four times the timeout.

Sample rows are a separate switch: when on, `describe` shows a few rows of each table. A call beyond the level is refused
with the level it needs. Ask the person to change a level; you can't.

## read-only

Statements you write run only when AirSQL's classifier proves them read-only: one statement, `SELECT`,
`WITH … SELECT`, `SHOW`, `DESCRIBE` or `EXPLAIN` (not `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`). It refuses `INTO`, `FOR UPDATE`,
`LOCK IN SHARE MODE`, optimizer hints, temporary tables, and functions such as `SLEEP`, `BENCHMARK`, `GET_LOCK`,
`LOAD_FILE` and stored functions. Each statement then runs on AirSQL's own agent session, which is read-only, inside
`START TRANSACTION READ ONLY` … `ROLLBACK`, with the server's statement timeout and a watchdog. Both guards always apply.
A refused statement comes back with `ok: false` and the reason; the other statements of the call still run.

## tools

- `context {}`: start here.
- `get_schema {connection, databases?, format?: compact | ddl, if_changed_from?}`: compact lines look like
  `orders: id bigint PK AI, customer_id int NULL → customers.id, total decimal(12,2) ='0.00'; KEY(customer_id)`:
  PK primary key, AI auto-increment, NULL nullable, `=` default, `→` foreign key, then composite keys and indexes, and
  `-- comment`. Views start with `view`, sequences with `sequence`. System databases are left out unless named. A
  database too big for the reply comes as names only: name it, or describe its tables.
- `describe {connection, objects: ["table" or "db.table"], database?}`: names in backquotes may contain dots.
- `run_queries {connection, database?, queries: [{sql, max_rows?}], format?: json | csv, to_file?}`: 200 rows per
  statement unless `max_rows` says more (up to the row cap); `capped: true` means there were more. Values are text
  (binary as 0x… hex), NULL is null in JSON and an empty field in CSV, long values are cut at 2,000 characters.
  `to_file: true` (analytics) writes each result to a CSV or JSON file in AirSQL's agent export folder and answers with
  its path, rows and size instead of the rows.
- `profile {connection, table, database?, columns?, where?}`: row count, and per column NULLs, distinct values, min,
  max, average (numbers) and the five most common values, computed on the server.
- `explain {connection, sql, database?, format?: traditional | json}`.
- `open_in_console {sql, title?, connection?}`: never runs anything.
- `read_console {tab?}`: by id or title from `context`; default the active console tab.
- `guide {topic?}`: this guide.

Long calls send progress notifications when your client asks for them (`_meta.progressToken`).

## resources

Each connected connection you may read has its compact schema as a resource, `airsql://<connection name>/schema`
(percent-encoded), the same text as `get_schema`. `resources/list` lists them.

## recipes

- **Answer a question about the data**: `context` → `get_schema` → `describe` the tables involved → `run_queries`
  with a `COUNT(*)` first, then the query, with `max_rows` small.
- **Analyse a big result**: with analytics, `run_queries` with `to_file: true`, then read the file with your own tools.
- **Change data or structure**: write the statements, then `open_in_console` with a clear title; tell the person what
  they do. After they run them, `read_console`.
- **Check a query's cost**: `explain` it, look for full scans (`type: ALL`) on big tables, `describe` for indexes.

## troubleshooting

- "isn't running, or agents are off": open AirSQL and turn on Settings ▸ Agents ▸ Allow AI agents to use AirSQL.
- "No connection … is open to agents": use a name or id from `context`; the person may have set it to Off.
- "isn't connected": ask the person to connect it in AirSQL.
- "needs Schema + read" (or analytics): the person can raise the level in Settings ▸ Agents.
- "Refused": the statement isn't provably read-only; rewrite it as one plain SELECT, or propose it with
  `open_in_console`.
- "Stopped at the agent timeout": narrow the query (WHERE, LIMIT), or ask for the analytics level.
